item.title: Hi Bill. Thank you for making the "hi" video, I really enjoyed it! Here is my working theory about it. Apologies if this reads like a badly written high school essay. I didn't plan to write down this much but I just needed to get my thoughts out of my head. Please feel free to ignore this if it's too much. I think the video is essentially about two parts of a single mind struggling to make sense of and say something about the world. The two parts are represented by not-shelby-person and Shelby, who have contrasting approaches to their understanding of and interactions with reality. Not-shelby-person and Shelby likely represent two parts of a single mind. When not-shelby-person begins to ask Shelby whether she has any mixtapes to be delivered, she instantly knows what is going to be asked and presents her mixtape. In the final song about the concert, the lyrics "i know, do you know?" are sung while both characters rapidly switch positions, representing a rapid conversation between two selves that are actually one person. The fact that not-shelby-person and Shelby are male and female also may allude to how both parts of the mind are needed to give birth two a new idea (represented by the 'concert'). Not-shelby-person has a very prescriptive approach in that he often tries to define and limit things. His hairstyle seems to resemble bricks, perhaps representing a desire to lay a foundation for his understanding of reality brick by brick. He attempts to know where he is, what things are, and how things are supposed to be. However, he fails at these attempts multiple times. He asks Shelby if her paper is double-sided, perhaps to know the full physical limit of her list. His attempt to define his location with the map ends up becoming self-referential ("a map of the map"). He says "trick or treat" at the door of the record company (isn't that what you're supposed to say at the door?) only to have to use the other door that says "use other door". He installs a second roof just to get it "taken care of". He also desires agency. His skateboard, which he controls with his legs, is representative of this. He doesn't get very far on it though, as seen when it gets stuck in a tree and when he keeps jumping back in place during his "good start" montage. Another image of stagnation is the clock, which doesn't seem to move past 10:14 throughout the video. He isn't oblivious to his failures, as in his "good start" montage he sings "I'm not sad, I don't feel bad", which could be him suppressing his true feelings or implying that he doesn't feel happy or good either. Due to not-shelby-person's obsession with (and failure at) defining and limiting the world into digestible chunks, he is in turn afraid of the "infinity bus", which represents the unlimited scope of the reality around him. The bus imagery evokes cyclical-ness (the wheels on the bus go round and round)and the loss of agency (you don't control the bus, as opposed to the skateboard). The bus appears three times: when he begins to plan his day, when he asks Shelby whether she wrote down the fact that she is writing everything down (self-referential), and after the final dialogue between not-shelby-person and Shelby (more on that later). All appearances occur when not-shelby-person starts to realize the unlimited and undefinable scope of everything. Shelby is almost a negation of not-shelby-person. She is very descriptive and observational, as seen in her writing down everything. Her hairstyle resembles planets, representing her interest in observing things in motion. She doesn't care about defining things with strict boundaries, as she ironically defines her definition-obsessed counterpart "not-shelby-person" (which by definition really could be anyone). But she also fails to capture every event, as she seemingly doesn't know where to start nor what to keep track of ("boats, roaring 20s, etc") and ends up becoming overwhelmed and scribbling everything. Of the 'concert', not-shelby-person says "Is that the concert we're supposed to write" (showing an active desire to do what he's supposed to), while Shelby replies "someone's gotta do it", showing her more passive nature. When working on the 'concert', not-shelby-person says he likes that "this doesn't go any further", pointing out the boundary of the paper. In response, Shelby says she likes "how it does go... as far as it does go". She then sings about wanting to know how far it goes, visualizing smaller and smaller waves until not-shelby-person stops her abruptly, perhaps a little scared by the infinite repetition. Shelby is willing to examine reality as it is without imposing any boundaries. This is why she doesn't seem to be afraid of the infinity buses. Her name "Shelby" might also be read as "shall be", as in, whatever shall be, shall be. Both not-shelby-person and Shelby want to understand and say something about the world, through either definitions and boundaries or through observation and record-keeping respectively. This reflects two types of interactions between the human mind and reality. Both of these interactions produce their own 'mixtapes' and their own projects (planning the day, writing down everything), which represent different approaches to making meaningful statements about reality. "Selling" is also a recurring theme, which could be read as the act of "selling" or convincing other people of a statement or observation of reality. The phone selling Shelby everything that she does ("got to go downstairs") might represent how phones, particularly through ads or social media, often try to convince others of a certain interpretation of their own reality. Both not-shelby-person and Shelby fail at "selling" their own interpretations of reality. Their mixtapes are received passively rather than enthusiastically by the record company. The concert, which becomes a collaborative project between the two, produces only adjectives ("great! amazing! wonderful!") and descriptions ("ends differently from how it starts" and "gets awards but still deserves more") with no grammatical subject, after which it quite literally falls flat. After witnessing this, the final dialogue ("I'd buy tickets to that!" "They don't sell tickets to that." "Sell tickets to what?" "Exactly.") confirms how "that" (the concert they had just witnessed) is undefinable and therefore cannot be "sold to" or be understood by others. Shelby's final statement "This must be why we're hiding in the basement" along with the shot of multiple infinity buses shows the futility of the mind's attempts at stating anything about reality without hiding from its boundless, undefinable scope.

item.title: love everything in the new video. does it feel great to 3D model so many details after the work is complete? it adds so much to my experience
item.description:
11.11.26 7:42 pm
Q: love everything in the new video. does it feel great to 3D model so many details after the work is complete? it adds so much to my experience
A: there is a spectrum of how much to model before camera, and how much to model after camera. this would be an example of an experiment to see what happens when you model just about everything before camera. The great advantage to this: when you finally show up with the camera, the world is your playground. you can find all kinds of groovy shots by putting the camera in all kinds of crazy places, and you find your shots based on all the great things that are there. The huge disadvantage is that it's extremely wasteful. you model so much stuff that will never be seen. It also has the tendency to make your camera look a little hyper, because you are desperately trying to show off all the cool stuff. The other end of the spectrum would be to model almost nothing (just basic blocks to indicate where things are), then do your camera, trying to imagine what could be there. then model things afterwards, playing only to the camera shots. this would obviously be way more efficient, but the disadvantage is that you don't get the magic of surprising yourself by what you see when you put the camera in different places. With this video (and many upcoming videos) i'm pretty sure i've figured out for sure that modeling everything before camera is not the best way to go. too wasteful. but it is a trade off
